notes.front: What is a policy definition in Azure Policy?
notes.back: A business rule with conditions that are enforced and an effect that takes place if the conditions are met.
notes.explanation: Every policy starts with one, and Azure Policy offers several built-in definitions by default.
notes.example: Like a club rule that states what is required and what happens if it is broken, but applied to Azure resources.
notes.source: Microsoft, “What is Azure Policy?”, “Policy definition” (MicrosoftDocs/azure-docs on GitHub)
notes.evidence: The journey to create and implement a policy in Azure Policy begins when you create a policy definition. Every policy definition has conditions that are enforced. And, it has a defined effect that takes place if the conditions are met. In Azure Policy, we offer several built-in policies that are available by default.

notes.front: What is an initiative definition in Azure Policy?
notes.back: A group of related policy definitions that you assign and manage as a single item.
notes.explanation: Rather than assigning each policy individually, you apply the initiative, which simplifies assignment and management.
notes.example: Like a playlist you start with one press instead of playing each song, but the songs are policy definitions.
notes.source: Microsoft, “Azure Policy initiative definition structure” (MicrosoftDocs/azure-docs on GitHub)
notes.evidence: Initiatives enable you to group several related policy definitions to simplify assignments and management because you work with a group as a single item. For example, you can group related tagging policy definitions into a single initiative. Rather than assigning each policy individually, you apply the initiative.

notes.front: What is a policy assignment?
notes.back: A policy definition or initiative that has been assigned to a specific scope.
notes.explanation: That scope can range from a management group down to an individual resource.
notes.example: Like pinning a notice to one particular noticeboard: the notice applies only where it is pinned.
notes.source: Microsoft, “What is Azure Policy?”, “Assignments” (MicrosoftDocs/azure-docs on GitHub)
notes.evidence: An assignment is a policy definition or initiative that was assigned to a specific scope. This scope could range from a management group to an individual resource.

notes.front: What are non-compliance messages on a policy assignment?
notes.back: Optional custom messages, set on the assignment, that describe why a resource is non-compliant.
notes.explanation: A custom message is shown in addition to the default non-compliance error message, not instead of it.
notes.example: Like a note on a locked door saying “Staff only: ask at reception”, alongside the plain buzz of a refused entry.
notes.source: Microsoft, “Azure Policy assignment structure”, “Non-compliance messages” (MicrosoftDocs/azure-docs on GitHub)
notes.evidence: To set a custom message that describes why a resource is non-compliant with the policy or initiative definition, set nonComplianceMessages in the assignment definition. This node is an array of message entries. This custom message is in addition to the default error message for non-compliance and is optional.

notes.front: What are assignment parameters in Azure Policy?
notes.back: Values that a policy assignment supplies for the parameters defined in its policy or initiative definition.
notes.explanation: They let you reuse one definition with different resources while checking for different business values or outcomes.
notes.example: Like a form letter with blanks: the letter is the definition, and each assignment fills in its own values.
notes.source: Microsoft, “Azure Policy assignment structure”, “Parameters” (MicrosoftDocs/azure-docs on GitHub)
notes.evidence: This segment of the policy assignment provides the values for the parameters defined in the policy definition or initiative definition. This design makes it possible to reuse a policy or initiative definition with different resources, but check for different business values or outcomes.

notes.front: What is a remediation task in Azure Policy?
notes.back: A task that brings existing non-compliant resources into compliance by deploying a `deployIfNotExists` template or applying `modify` operations.
notes.explanation: It works whether the assignment is on a management group, a subscription, a resource group or an individual resource.
notes.example: Like a repair crew sent after an inspection to fix houses already built, rather than an inspector who only stops new ones.
notes.source: Microsoft, “Remediate non-compliant resources with Azure Policy” (MicrosoftDocs/azure-docs on GitHub)
notes.evidence: Remediation is accomplished through remediation tasks that deploy the deployIfNotExists template or the modify operations of the assigned policy on your existing resources and subscriptions, whether that assignment is on a management group, subscription, resource group, or individual resource.

notes.front: What does a CanNotDelete lock do?
notes.back: Authorised users can still read and modify the resource, but they can’t delete it.
notes.explanation: Unlike a ReadOnly lock, it still lets authorised users update the resource.
notes.example: Like a filing cabinet whose drawers open for editing but which is bolted to the floor.
notes.source: Microsoft, “Lock your Azure resources to protect your infrastructure” (MicrosoftDocs/azure-docs on GitHub)
notes.evidence: - **CanNotDelete** means authorized users can read and modify a resource, but they can't delete it. - **ReadOnly** means authorized users can read a resource, but they can't delete or update it.

notes.front: What does a ReadOnly lock do?
notes.back: Authorised users can read the resource but can’t delete or update it.
notes.explanation: Applying it is similar to restricting all authorised users to the permissions that the Reader role provides.
notes.example: Like a glass display case: everyone can look, but nobody can move or change the exhibit.
notes.source: Microsoft, “Lock your Azure resources to protect your infrastructure” (MicrosoftDocs/azure-docs on GitHub)
notes.evidence: **ReadOnly** means authorized users can read a resource, but they can't delete or update it. Applying this lock is similar to restricting all authorized users to the permissions that the **Reader** role provides.

notes.front: What is Microsoft Cost Management?
notes.back: A suite of tools that help organisations analyse, monitor and optimise their Microsoft Cloud costs.
notes.explanation: Anyone with access to a billing account, subscription, resource group or management group can use it.
notes.example: Like a household budgeting app, but for an organisation’s cloud bills.
notes.source: Microsoft, “What is Microsoft Cost Management” (MicrosoftDocs/azure-docs on GitHub)
notes.evidence: Microsoft Cost Management is a suite of FinOps tools that help organizations analyze, monitor, and optimize their Microsoft Cloud costs. Cost Management is available to anyone with access to a billing account, subscription, resource group, or management group.

notes.front: What is a budget in Cost Management?
notes.back: A feature that helps you plan for and drive accountability for spending, with alerts based on actual or forecast cost.
notes.explanation: It lets you proactively tell others about their spending and monitor how spending progresses over time.
notes.example: Like a monthly spending limit you set in a banking app, which messages you as your spending approaches it.
notes.source: Microsoft, “Tutorial: Create and manage budgets” (MicrosoftDocs/azure-docs on GitHub)
notes.evidence: Budgets in Cost Management help you plan for and drive organizational accountability. They help you proactively inform others about their spending to manage costs and monitor how spending progresses over time. You can configure alerts based on your actual cost or forecasted cost to ensure that your spending is within your organizational spending limit.

notes.front: What is the root management group?
notes.back: The single top-level management group in each directory, into which all management groups and subscriptions fold up.
notes.explanation: It allows global policies and Azure role assignments to be applied at the directory level.
notes.example: Like the trunk of a family tree, from which every branch descends.
notes.source: Microsoft, “What are Azure management groups?”, “Root management group for each directory” (MicrosoftDocs/azure-docs on GitHub)
notes.evidence: Each directory has a single top-level management group called the root management group. The root management group is built into the hierarchy to have all management groups and subscriptions fold up to it. The root management group allows for the application of global policies and Azure role assignments at the directory level.

notes.front: How does Azure Policy decide whether a resource is compliant?
notes.back: It compares the resource’s properties with business rules, which are known as policy definitions.
notes.explanation: It evaluates actions taken in Azure as well as the resources themselves.
notes.source: Microsoft, “What is Azure Policy?”, “Overview” (MicrosoftDocs/azure-docs on GitHub)
notes.evidence: Azure Policy evaluates resources and actions in Azure by comparing the properties of those resources to business rules. These business rules, described in JSON format, are known as policy definitions.

notes.front: Besides resource changes and new or updated assignments, Azure Policy evaluates resources in a standard compliance cycle that occurs once every {{c1::24 hours}}.
notes.explanation: New assignments and updates to assigned policies or initiatives also trigger evaluation.
notes.source: Microsoft, “What is Azure Policy?”, “Understand evaluation outcomes” (MicrosoftDocs/azure-docs on GitHub)
notes.evidence: - A scope gets a new assignment of a policy or initiative. - A policy or initiative already assigned to a scope is updated. - The standard compliance evaluation cycle that occurs once every 24 hours.

notes.front: Which built-in policy definition restricts the locations available for new resources, and what is its effect?
notes.back: Allowed Locations, with the Deny effect.
notes.explanation: Its effect is used to enforce geo-compliance requirements.
notes.source: Microsoft, “What is Azure Policy?”, “Policy definition” (MicrosoftDocs/azure-docs on GitHub)
notes.evidence: **Allowed Locations** (Deny): Restricts the available locations for new resources. Its effect is used to enforce your geo-compliance requirements.

notes.front: Deployments keep arriving without a required tag. You want the tag and a default value added whenever a request leaves it out. Which built-in policy, with which effect, fits?
notes.back: Add a tag to resources, with the Modify effect.
notes.explanation: It applies the required tag and its default value only when the deploy request doesn’t specify it.
notes.source: Microsoft, “What is Azure Policy?”, “Policy definition” (MicrosoftDocs/azure-docs on GitHub)
notes.evidence: **Add a tag to resources** (Modify): Applies a required tag and its default value if the deploy request doesn't specify it.

notes.front: One policy definition checks the value of a cost-centre tag. Two departments need different values checked. Do you need two policy definitions?
notes.back: No. Assign the same definition twice, giving each assignment its own parameter value.
notes.explanation: Reusing one definition with different parameters reduces the duplication and complexity of policy definitions.
notes.source: Microsoft, “Azure Policy assignment structure”, “Parameters” (MicrosoftDocs/azure-docs on GitHub)
notes.evidence: The same policy definition is reusable with a different set of parameters for a different department, reducing the duplication and complexity of policy definitions while providing flexibility.

notes.front: You are starting with a single policy definition but expect to add similar ones later. What does Microsoft recommend you create and assign?
notes.back: An initiative definition containing it, even though it holds only one definition for now.
notes.explanation: You can then add policy definitions to the initiative later without increasing the number of assignments to manage.
notes.source: Microsoft, “What is Azure Policy?”, “Recommendations for managing policies” (MicrosoftDocs/azure-docs on GitHub)
notes.evidence: We recommend creating and assigning initiative definitions even if starting with a single policy definition. This method enables you to add policy definitions to the initiative later without increasing the number of assignments to manage.

notes.front: A policy definition is assigned to a resource group. Does it apply to the resources inside that group?
notes.back: Yes. All child resources inherit the assignments.
notes.explanation: You can, however, exclude a subscope from the assignment.
notes.source: Microsoft, “What is Azure Policy?”, “Assignments” (MicrosoftDocs/azure-docs on GitHub)
notes.evidence: All child resources inherit the assignments. This design means that a definition applied to a resource group is also applied to resources in that resource group. However, you can exclude a subscope from the assignment.

notes.front: A subscription-level assignment denies every resource type not on an approved list. For one resource group you assign a longer list, but the extra types are still denied. What should you do?
notes.back: Exclude that resource group from the subscription-level assignment, then assign the more permissive definition to it.
notes.explanation: Azure Policy is an explicit deny system: the only way to allow a denied resource is to modify the denying assignment.
notes.source: Microsoft, “What is Azure Policy?”, “Assignments” (MicrosoftDocs/azure-docs on GitHub)
notes.evidence: Azure Policy is an explicit deny system. Instead, you need to exclude the child management group or subscription from the management group-level assignment. Then, assign the more permissive definition on the child management group or subscription level. If any assignment results in a resource getting denied, then the only way to allow the resource is to modify the denying assignment.

notes.front: A policy is assigned at a management group. At which levels are resources actually evaluated?
notes.back: Only resources at the subscription or resource group level.
notes.explanation: Assigning at the management group level is allowed; it is the evaluation that happens lower down.
notes.source: Microsoft, “What is Azure Policy?”, “Resources covered by Azure Policy” (MicrosoftDocs/azure-docs on GitHub)
notes.evidence: Although a policy can be assigned at the management group level, only resources at the subscription or resource group level are evaluated.

notes.front: How many effects does each policy definition have, and what does the effect decide?
notes.back: A single effect, which decides what happens when the policy rule is evaluated to match.
notes.explanation: Effects behave differently for a new resource, an updated resource and an existing resource.
notes.source: Microsoft, “Azure Policy definitions effect basics” (MicrosoftDocs/azure-docs on GitHub)
notes.evidence: Each policy definition in Azure Policy has a single `effect` in its `policyRule`. That `effect` determines what happens when the policy rule is evaluated to match. The effects behave differently if they are for a new resource, an updated resource, or an existing resource.

notes.front: In Azure Policy’s order of evaluation, which effect is checked first, and why?
notes.back: `disabled`, to determine whether the policy rule should be evaluated at all.
notes.explanation: Only after that check are the other effects evaluated.
notes.source: Microsoft, “Azure Policy definitions effect basics”, “Order of evaluation” (MicrosoftDocs/azure-docs on GitHub)
notes.evidence: - disabled is checked first to determine whether the policy rule should be evaluated.

notes.front: Why does Azure Policy evaluate `deny` before `audit`?
notes.back: To prevent double logging of an undesired resource.
notes.explanation: After deny come audit and then manual in the order.
notes.source: Microsoft, “Azure Policy definitions effect basics”, “Order of evaluation” (MicrosoftDocs/azure-docs on GitHub)
notes.evidence: deny is then evaluated. By evaluating deny before audit, double logging of an undesired resource is prevented. - audit is evaluated. - manual is evaluated.

notes.front: Which two effects evaluate after the Resource Provider returns a success code on a Resource Manager mode request?
notes.back: `auditIfNotExists` and `deployIfNotExists`.
notes.explanation: They determine whether more compliance logging or action is required.
notes.source: Microsoft, “Azure Policy definitions effect basics”, “Order of evaluation” (MicrosoftDocs/azure-docs on GitHub)
notes.evidence: After the Resource Provider returns a success code on a Resource Manager mode request, auditIfNotExists and deployIfNotExists evaluate to determine whether more compliance logging or action is required.

notes.front: You are rolling out a new policy and don’t know how it will affect scripts that autoscale your applications. Which effects does Microsoft suggest starting with?
notes.back: `audit` or `auditIfNotExists`, rather than an enforcement effect such as `deny`, `modify` or `deployIfNotExists`.
notes.explanation: An enforcement effect might hinder automation tasks already in place, such as autoscaling scripts.
notes.source: Microsoft, “What is Azure Policy?”, “Recommendations for managing policies” (MicrosoftDocs/azure-docs on GitHub)
notes.evidence: Start with an `audit` or `auditIfNotExists` effect instead of an enforcement (`deny`, `modify`, `deployIfNotExists`) effect to track how your policy definition affects the resources in your environment. If you have scripts already in place to autoscale your applications, setting an enforcement effect might hinder such automation tasks already in place.

notes.front: A subscription assignment denies resources without an owner tag. A resource group assignment in it denies resources without a cost-centre tag. A new resource in that group has only the owner tag. What happens?
notes.back: It is denied: layered assignments are cumulative most restrictive.
notes.explanation: Each assignment is evaluated on its own, so a resource can’t slip through a gap from differences in scope.
notes.source: Microsoft, “Azure Policy definitions effect basics”, “Layering policy definitions” (MicrosoftDocs/azure-docs on GitHub)
notes.evidence: Each assignment is individually evaluated. As such, there isn't an opportunity for a resource to slip through a gap from differences in scope. The net result of layering policy definitions is considered to be **cumulative most restrictive**.

notes.front: Azure Policy versus Azure role-based access control: what does each govern?
notes.back: Role-based access control: which actions users may take at each scope. Azure Policy: whether the resulting resource complies.
notes.explanation: Even when a user may perform an action, Azure Policy still blocks the create or update if the result would be non-compliant.
notes.source: Microsoft, “What is Azure Policy?”, “Azure Policy and Azure RBAC” (MicrosoftDocs/azure-docs on GitHub)
notes.evidence: Azure RBAC focuses on managing user actions at different scopes. If control of an action is required based on user information, then Azure RBAC is the correct tool to use. Even if an individual has access to perform an action, if the result is a non-compliant resource, Azure Policy still blocks the create or update.

notes.front: A user holds Contributor on a resource group and creates a resource that an assigned deny policy forbids. What happens?
notes.back: Azure Policy blocks the create, even though the user has permission to perform the action.
notes.explanation: Used together, role-based access control and Azure Policy give full scope control in Azure.
notes.source: Microsoft, “What is Azure Policy?”, “Azure Policy and Azure RBAC” (MicrosoftDocs/azure-docs on GitHub)
notes.evidence: Even if an individual has access to perform an action, if the result is a non-compliant resource, Azure Policy still blocks the create or update. The combination of Azure RBAC and Azure Policy provides full scope control in Azure.

notes.front: Which built-in role includes most Azure Policy operations?
notes.back: Resource Policy Contributor.
notes.explanation: Owner has full rights, while Contributor and Reader can use all read operations.
notes.source: Microsoft, “What is Azure Policy?”, “Azure RBAC permissions in Azure Policy” (MicrosoftDocs/azure-docs on GitHub)
notes.evidence: Many built-in roles grant permission to Azure Policy resources. The **Resource Policy Contributor** role includes most Azure Policy operations. **Owner** has full rights. Both **Contributor** and **Reader** have access to all _read_ Azure Policy operations.

notes.front: A user with only the Contributor role wants to create a new policy assignment. Can they?
notes.back: No. Contributor might trigger remediation but can’t create or update definitions and assignments.
notes.explanation: Granting a `deployIfNotExists` or `modify` assignment’s managed identity its permissions needs User Access Administrator.
notes.source: Microsoft, “What is Azure Policy?”, “Azure RBAC permissions in Azure Policy” (MicrosoftDocs/azure-docs on GitHub)
notes.evidence: **Contributor** might trigger resource remediation, but can't _create_ or _update_ definitions and assignments. **User Access Administrator** is necessary to grant the managed identity on deployIfNotExists or modify assignments necessary permissions.

notes.front: Enforcement mode `Default` versus `DoNotEnforce`: what happens to the policy effect during resource creation or update?
notes.back: Default: the effect is enforced. DoNotEnforce: the effect isn’t enforced, and no Activity log entry is written.
notes.explanation: In both modes you can still remediate manually.
notes.source: Microsoft, “Azure Policy assignment structure”, “Enforcement mode” (MicrosoftDocs/azure-docs on GitHub)
notes.evidence: |Enabled |Default |string |Yes |Yes |The policy effect is enforced during resource creation or update. | |Disabled |DoNotEnforce |string |Yes |No | The policy effect isn't enforced during resource creation or update. |

notes.front: You want to see which resources a new deny assignment would affect before it blocks anyone. Which enforcement mode do you set?
notes.back: `DoNotEnforce`.
notes.choices:
A) Default
B) DoNotEnforce
C) Remove the assignment’s effect
D) Add the resources to notScopes
notes.choicesExplained: A enforces the effect at once. C is not an enforcement mode, and the rule still needs its effect to be judged. D excludes resources, so they would not be evaluated at all.
notes.explanation: The mode is meant for testing a new assignment and reviewing its compliance impact before the effect is enforced.
notes.source: Microsoft, “Azure Policy assignment structure”, “Enforcement mode” (MicrosoftDocs/azure-docs on GitHub)
notes.evidence: Use DoNotEnforce when you want to evaluate the policy assignment before enforcement. This mode is useful for testing a new assignment, reviewing compliance impact, or validating policy logic before the policy effect is enforced.

notes.front: What is the `notScopes` property of a policy assignment?
notes.back: An array of child resource containers or resources excluded from the assignment’s evaluation.
notes.explanation: It can be added or updated after the assignment is created, and an excluded resource is different from an exempted one.
notes.source: Microsoft, “Azure Policy assignment structure”, “Excluded scopes” (MicrosoftDocs/azure-docs on GitHub)
notes.evidence: This property is an array to enable excluding one or more resource containers or resources from evaluation. notScopes can be added or updated after creation of the initial assignment. > [!NOTE] > An excluded resource is different from an exempted resource.

notes.front: A subscription-wide assignment requires a cost-centre tag, but one resource group holds a supplier’s test resources that can’t be tagged. How do you keep the policy for everything else?
notes.back: Add that resource group to the assignment’s excluded scopes (`notScopes`).
notes.explanation: An assignment’s scope otherwise includes all its child resource containers and child resources.
notes.source: Microsoft, “Azure Policy assignment structure”, “Excluded scopes” (MicrosoftDocs/azure-docs on GitHub)
notes.evidence: The scope of the assignment includes all child resource containers and child resources. If a child resource container or child resource shouldn't have the definition applied, each can be excluded from evaluation by setting `notScopes`.

notes.front: Resources that don’t comply with policies using which two effects can be put right through remediation?
notes.back: `deployIfNotExists` and `modify`.
notes.explanation: Remediation tasks deploy the deployIfNotExists template or apply the modify operations to existing resources.
notes.source: Microsoft, “Remediate non-compliant resources with Azure Policy” (MicrosoftDocs/azure-docs on GitHub)
notes.evidence: Resources that are non-compliant to policies with deployIfNotExists or modify effects can be put into a compliant state through **Remediation**. Remediation is accomplished through **remediation tasks** that deploy the deployIfNotExists template or the modify operations of the assigned policy on your existing resources and subscriptions

notes.front: An assignment with the `audit` effect shows forty non-compliant storage accounts. Will it appear among the policies you can remediate?
notes.back: No. The Policies to remediate tab shows deployIfNotExists and modify assignments; audit isn’t a remediable effect.
notes.explanation: You open a new remediation task by selecting one of those assignments that has non-compliant resources.
notes.source: Microsoft, “Remediate non-compliant resources with Azure Policy”, “Option 1: Create a remediation task from the Remediation page” (MicrosoftDocs/azure-docs on GitHub)
notes.evidence: All deployIfNotExists and modify policy assignments are shown on the **Policies to remediate** tab. Select one with resources that are non-compliant to open the **New remediation task** page.

notes.front: How many `deployIfNotExists` or `modify` policies can a single remediation task remediate?
notes.back: One at a time.
notes.explanation: For an initiative assignment, you pick the one policy to remediate from a drop-down.
notes.source: Microsoft, “Remediate non-compliant resources with Azure Policy”, “Step 2: Specify remediation task details” (MicrosoftDocs/azure-docs on GitHub)
notes.evidence: If the remediation task is initiated from an initiative assignment, select the policy to remediate from the drop-down. One deployIfNotExists or modify policy can be remediated through a single Remediation task at a time.

notes.front: Whose identity does Azure Policy use to deploy or modify resources during remediation?
notes.back: The managed identity associated with the policy assignment.
notes.explanation: That applies both to template deployments for deployIfNotExists and to resource changes for modify.
notes.source: Microsoft, “Remediate non-compliant resources with Azure Policy”, “How remediation access control works” (MicrosoftDocs/azure-docs on GitHub)
notes.evidence: When Azure Policy starts a template deployment when evaluating deployIfNotExists policies or modifies a resource when evaluating modify policies, it does so using a managed identity associated with the policy assignment.

notes.front: You create a `deployIfNotExists` assignment with Azure PowerShell, and its remediation deployments fail for lack of permissions. Why?
notes.back: Outside the portal, the assignment’s managed identity must be granted its roles manually; only the portal grants them automatically.
notes.explanation: Without those roles, the remediation deployment fails.
notes.source: Microsoft, “Remediate non-compliant resources with Azure Policy”, “Grant permissions to the managed identity through defined roles” (MicrosoftDocs/azure-docs on GitHub)
notes.evidence: it will be granted permissions automatically only through the portal. You may skip this step if creating a managed identity through the portal. For all other methods, the assignment's managed identity must be manually granted access through the addition of roles, or else the remediation deployment will fail.

notes.front: How many managed identities can one policy assignment have?
notes.back: One, system-assigned or user-assigned, though that identity can hold more than one role.
notes.explanation: Assignments with the deployIfNotExists or modify effect need this identity to remediate non-compliant resources.
notes.source: Microsoft, “Azure Policy assignment structure”, “Identity” (MicrosoftDocs/azure-docs on GitHub)
notes.evidence: Policy assignments with effect set to deployIfNotExists or modify must have an identity property to do remediation on non-compliant resources. A single policy assignment can be associated with only one system-assigned or user-assigned managed identity. However, that identity can be assigned more than one role if necessary.

notes.front: Your `deployIfNotExists` policy is assigned at a management group. Should you create its remediation task in the assignment wizard?
notes.back: No. That option suits subscription assignments; for a management group, create it afterwards from the Remediation page or the non-compliant assignment.
notes.explanation: Where it is supported, creating the task in the wizard is the most streamlined approach.
notes.source: Microsoft, “Remediate non-compliant resources with Azure Policy”, “Option 3: Create a remediation task during policy assignment” (MicrosoftDocs/azure-docs on GitHub)
notes.evidence: This is the most streamlined approach for creating a remediation task and is supported for policies assigned on a _subscription_. For policies assigned on a _management group_, remediation tasks should be created using Option 1 or Option 2 after evaluation has determined resource compliance.

notes.front: Management locks versus role-based access control: whom does each restrict?
notes.back: A lock applies its restriction across all users and roles; role-based access control sets permissions for particular users and roles.
notes.explanation: A lock restricts everyone at once rather than granting or denying access per user.
notes.source: Microsoft, “Lock your Azure resources to protect your infrastructure” (MicrosoftDocs/azure-docs on GitHub)
notes.evidence: Unlike with role-based access control (RBAC), you use management locks to apply a restriction across all users and roles.

notes.front: What are CanNotDelete and ReadOnly locks called in the Azure portal?
notes.back: Delete and Read-only.
notes.explanation: CanNotDelete and ReadOnly are the command-line names for the same two locks.
notes.source: Microsoft, “Lock your Azure resources to protect your infrastructure” (MicrosoftDocs/azure-docs on GitHub)
notes.evidence: In the portal, these locks are called **Delete** and **Read-only**. In the command line, these locks are called **CanNotDelete** and **ReadOnly**.

notes.front: When adding a lock to a resource group in the portal, which three fields do you fill in?
notes.back: Lock name, Lock type and Notes.
notes.explanation: The lock types on offer are Read-only and Delete.
notes.source: Microsoft, “Use the Azure portal and Azure Resource Manager to manage resource groups”, “Lock resource groups” (MicrosoftDocs/azure-docs on GitHub)
notes.evidence: 1. In the left pane, select **Locks**. 1. To add a lock to the resource group, select **Add**. 1. Enter **Lock name**, **Lock type**, and **Notes**. The lock types include **Read-only** and **Delete**.

notes.front: Administrators must keep changing a production database’s settings, but it must never be deleted by accident. Which lock fits?
notes.back: A CanNotDelete lock.
notes.explanation: It still lets authorised users read and modify the resource.
notes.source: Microsoft, “Lock your Azure resources to protect your infrastructure” (MicrosoftDocs/azure-docs on GitHub)
notes.evidence: - **CanNotDelete** means authorized users can read and modify a resource, but they can't delete it.

notes.front: For an audit, a resource group’s configuration must stay exactly as it is for a month, whatever roles people hold. Which lock fits?
notes.back: A ReadOnly lock.
notes.explanation: It restricts all authorised users much as the Reader role would.
notes.source: Microsoft, “Lock your Azure resources to protect your infrastructure” (MicrosoftDocs/azure-docs on GitHub)
notes.evidence: **ReadOnly** means authorized users can read a resource, but they can't delete or update it. Applying this lock is similar to restricting all authorized users to the permissions that the **Reader** role provides.

notes.front: A lock is applied to a resource group. Do resources added to the group later inherit it?
notes.back: Yes. All resources in the scope inherit the lock, including ones added later.
notes.explanation: Where several locks are inherited, the most restrictive one takes precedence.
notes.source: Microsoft, “Lock your Azure resources to protect your infrastructure”, “Lock inheritance” (MicrosoftDocs/azure-docs on GitHub)
notes.evidence: When you apply a lock at a parent scope, all resources within that scope inherit the same lock. Even resources you add later inherit the same parent lock. The most restrictive lock in the inheritance chain takes precedence.

notes.front: A subscription has a CanNotDelete lock and one of its resource groups has a ReadOnly lock. What can authorised users do to a resource in that group?
notes.back: Only read it.
notes.choices:
A) Read, modify and delete it
B) Read and modify it, but not delete it
C) Only read it
D) Nothing: locked resources can’t be read
notes.choicesExplained: A ignores both locks. B applies only the weaker CanNotDelete lock. D is wrong because both lock types still allow reading.
notes.explanation: Both locks are inherited, and the most restrictive lock in the chain, ReadOnly, takes precedence.
notes.source: Microsoft, “Lock your Azure resources to protect your infrastructure”, “Lock inheritance” (MicrosoftDocs/azure-docs on GitHub)
notes.evidence: Even resources you add later inherit the same parent lock. The most restrictive lock in the inheritance chain takes precedence.

notes.front: One resource in a resource group has a Delete lock; the group and its other resources are unlocked. What happens when you delete the resource group?
notes.back: Nothing is deleted: the whole delete operation is blocked.
notes.explanation: A partial deletion isn’t possible, so even the unlocked resources stay.
notes.source: Microsoft, “Lock your Azure resources to protect your infrastructure”, “Lock inheritance” (MicrosoftDocs/azure-docs on GitHub)
notes.evidence: If you have a **Delete** lock on a resource and attempt to delete its resource group, the feature blocks the whole delete operation. Even if the resource group or other resources in the resource group are unlocked, the deletion doesn't happen. A partial deletion isn't possible.

notes.front: Do locks apply to data plane operations?
notes.back: No. Locks apply only to control plane operations.
notes.explanation: Control plane requests go to management.azure.com; data plane requests go to your service instance itself.
notes.source: Microsoft, “Lock your Azure resources to protect your infrastructure”, “Understand scope of locks” (MicrosoftDocs/azure-docs on GitHub)
notes.evidence: Locks only apply to control plane Azure operations and not to data plane operations. Azure control plane operations go to `https://management.azure.com`. Azure data plane operations go to your service instance, such as `https://myaccount.blob.core.windows.net/`.

notes.front: A database server has a ReadOnly lock. Can applications still insert and delete rows in its databases?
notes.back: Yes. The lock protects the server from deletion or changes, not from data transactions.
notes.explanation: Locks protect a resource from changes but don’t restrict how the resource performs its functions.
notes.source: Microsoft, “Lock your Azure resources to protect your infrastructure”, “Understand scope of locks” (MicrosoftDocs/azure-docs on GitHub)
notes.evidence: The distinction means locks protect a resource from changes, but they don't restrict how a resource performs its functions. For example, a ReadOnly lock on an SQL Database logical server protects it from deletions or modifications. It allows you to create, update, or delete data in the server database.

notes.front: After a ReadOnly lock is put on a storage account, a user can no longer list its account keys. Why?
notes.back: Locks block `POST` requests that send data to Azure Resource Manager, and listing the keys is one of the blocked operations.
notes.explanation: Some operations that don’t seem to modify a resource still need actions that locks block.
notes.source: Microsoft, “Lock your Azure resources to protect your infrastructure”, “Considerations before applying your locks” (MicrosoftDocs/azure-docs on GitHub)
notes.evidence: Some operations that don't seem to modify a resource require blocked actions. Locks prevent the POST method from sending data to the Azure Resource Manager API. Some common examples of blocked operations are: - A read-only lock on a **storage account** prevents users from listing the account keys.

notes.front: A ReadOnly lock is placed on a resource group that holds virtual machines. What can’t users now do to the machines?
notes.back: Start or restart them.
notes.explanation: Those operations need a `POST` request, which the lock blocks for all users.
notes.source: Microsoft, “Lock your Azure resources to protect your infrastructure”, “Considerations before applying your locks” (MicrosoftDocs/azure-docs on GitHub)
notes.evidence: A read-only lock on a **resource group** that contains a **virtual machine** prevents all users from starting or restarting a virtual machine. These operations require a POST method request.

notes.front: Does a ReadOnly or CanNotDelete lock on a storage account protect the data in its blobs, queues, tables and files?
notes.back: No. It doesn’t protect the account’s data from being deleted or modified.
notes.explanation: The lock covers the storage account resource, not the data inside it.
notes.source: Microsoft, “Lock your Azure resources to protect your infrastructure”, “Considerations before applying your locks” (MicrosoftDocs/azure-docs on GitHub)
notes.evidence: A read-only lock or cannot-delete lock on a **storage account** doesn't protect its data from being deleted or modified. It also doesn't protect the data in a blob, queue, table, or file.

notes.front: Which two built-in roles have the access needed to create or delete management locks?
notes.back: Owner and User Access Administrator.
notes.explanation: Locks need access to the `Microsoft.Authorization/*` or `Microsoft.Authorization/locks/*` actions.
notes.source: Microsoft, “Lock your Azure resources to protect your infrastructure”, “Who can create or delete locks” (MicrosoftDocs/azure-docs on GitHub)
notes.evidence: To create or delete management locks, you need access to Microsoft.Authorization/* or Microsoft.Authorization/locks/* actions. Users assigned to the **Owner** and the **User Access Administrator** roles have the required access.

notes.front: An engineer is refused when trying to remove a Delete lock. Which role, or what alternative, would give the engineer the access?
notes.back: Owner or User Access Administrator, or a custom role with the required permissions.
notes.explanation: Some specialised built-in roles also grant this access.
notes.source: Microsoft, “Lock your Azure resources to protect your infrastructure”, “Who can create or delete locks” (MicrosoftDocs/azure-docs on GitHub)
notes.evidence: Users assigned to the **Owner** and the **User Access Administrator** roles have the required access. Some specialized built-in roles also grant this access. You can create a custom role with the required permissions.

notes.front: You tag a resource group. Do the resources inside it inherit the tag?
notes.back: No. Resources don’t inherit the tags applied to a resource group or a subscription.
notes.explanation: Policy definitions for tag compliance are the way to apply those tags to the resources.
notes.source: Microsoft, “Use tags to organize your Azure resources and management hierarchy”, “Inherit tags” (MicrosoftDocs/azure-docs on GitHub)
notes.evidence: Resources don't inherit the tags you apply to a resource group or a subscription. To apply tags from a subscription or resource group to the resources, see Assign policy definitions for tag compliance.

notes.front: Every new cost-accruing resource in a subscription must be provisioned with a Department tag. What should you use?
notes.back: One of the Azure Policy tag policies.
notes.explanation: Tag policies ensure that cost-accruing services are provisioned with a tag.
notes.source: Microsoft, “Use tags to organize your Azure resources and management hierarchy”, “Tag usage and recommendations” (MicrosoftDocs/azure-docs on GitHub)
notes.evidence: Resource tags support all cost-accruing services. To ensure that cost-accruing services are provisioned with a tag, use one of the tag policies.

notes.front: How many tag name-value pairs can one resource have?
notes.back: Up to 50.
notes.explanation: The same maximum applies to each resource group and each subscription.
notes.source: Microsoft, “Use tags to organize your Azure resources and management hierarchy”, “Limitations” (MicrosoftDocs/azure-docs on GitHub)
notes.evidence: Each resource, resource group, and subscription can have a maximum of 50 tag name-value pairs.

notes.front: You need more pieces of metadata on one resource than the tag limit allows. How can you store them?
notes.back: Put several values into one tag, using a JavaScript Object Notation string as the tag value.
notes.explanation: That one string can hold many of the values you would otherwise give separate tag names.
notes.source: Microsoft, “Use tags to organize your Azure resources and management hierarchy”, “Limitations” (MicrosoftDocs/azure-docs on GitHub)
notes.evidence: If you need to apply more tags than the maximum allowed number, use a JSON string for the tag value. The JSON string can contain many of the values that you apply to a single tag name.

notes.front: Can you apply tags to a management group?
notes.back: No. Tags can go on resources, resource groups and subscriptions, but not on management groups.
notes.explanation: The subscription is the highest level you can tag.
notes.source: Microsoft, “Use tags to organize your Azure resources and management hierarchy”, “Tag usage and recommendations” (MicrosoftDocs/azure-docs on GitHub)
notes.evidence: You can apply tags to your Azure resources, resource groups, and subscriptions but not to management groups.

notes.front: Are tag names and tag values case-sensitive?
notes.back: Tag names are case-insensitive for operations; tag values are case-sensitive.
notes.explanation: The resource provider might still keep the casing you give a tag name, and cost reports show it.
notes.source: Microsoft, “Use tags to organize your Azure resources and management hierarchy”, “Tag usage and recommendations” (MicrosoftDocs/azure-docs on GitHub)
notes.evidence: Tag names are case-insensitive for operations. An operation updates or retrieves a tag with a tag name, regardless of the casing. However, the resource provider might keep the casing you provide for the tag name. You see that casing in cost reports. Tag values are case-sensitive.

notes.front: Which built-in role lets you tag any resource, even without access to the resource itself?
notes.back: Tag Contributor.
notes.explanation: It grants write access to the `Microsoft.Resources/tags` resource type rather than to the resources.
notes.source: Microsoft, “Use tags to organize your Azure resources and management hierarchy”, “Required access” (MicrosoftDocs/azure-docs on GitHub)
notes.evidence: You can have write access to the Microsoft.Resources/tags resource type. This access lets you tag any resource, even if you don't have access to the resource itself. The Tag Contributor role grants this access.

notes.front: Three departments share a subscription’s virtual machines, and finance wants the usage split by department in the billing data. What should you use?
notes.back: Tags, which you can use to group billing data such as usage by cost centre.
notes.explanation: Tags can also categorise costs by runtime environment, such as production.
notes.source: Microsoft, “Use tags to organize your Azure resources and management hierarchy”, “Tags and billing” (MicrosoftDocs/azure-docs on GitHub)
notes.evidence: Use tags to group your billing data. For example, if you're running multiple virtual machines for different organizations, use the tags to group usage by cost center. You can also use tags to categorize costs by runtime environment, including the billing usage for virtual machines running in the production environment.

notes.front: What does the location you choose for a resource group determine?
notes.back: Where the resource group’s metadata about its resources is stored.
notes.explanation: For compliance reasons, you might need that metadata stored in a particular region.
notes.source: Microsoft, “Use the Azure portal and Azure Resource Manager to manage resource groups”, “What is a resource group” (MicrosoftDocs/azure-docs on GitHub)
notes.evidence: The resource group stores metadata about the resources. When you specify a location for the resource group, you're specifying where that metadata is stored. For compliance reasons, you might need to ensure that your data is stored in a particular region.

notes.front: A resource group was created in one Azure region. Must every resource in it be in that same region?
notes.back: No. Resources inside a resource group can be in different regions.
notes.explanation: The group’s location only fixes where its metadata is stored.
notes.source: Microsoft, “Use the Azure portal and Azure Resource Manager to manage resource groups”, “What is a resource group” (MicrosoftDocs/azure-docs on GitHub)
notes.evidence: When you specify a location for the resource group, you're specifying where that metadata is stored. For compliance reasons, you might need to ensure that your data is stored in a particular region. Resources inside a resource group can be in different regions.

notes.front: A web app, its database and its storage are always deployed, updated and retired together. How does Microsoft generally advise grouping them?
notes.back: In the same resource group, since they share the same lifecycle.
notes.explanation: You can then deploy, update and delete them as a group.
notes.source: Microsoft, “Use the Azure portal and Azure Resource Manager to manage resource groups”, “What is a resource group” (MicrosoftDocs/azure-docs on GitHub)
notes.evidence: Generally, add resources sharing the same lifecycle to the same resource group so you can easily deploy, update, and delete them as a group.

notes.front: When creating a resource group in the portal, which three values do you enter?
notes.back: The subscription, a new resource group name and the region.
notes.explanation: For the region you select an Azure location.
notes.source: Microsoft, “Use the Azure portal and Azure Resource Manager to manage resource groups”, “Create resource groups” (MicrosoftDocs/azure-docs on GitHub)
notes.evidence: - **Subscription**: Select your Azure subscription. - **Resource group**: Enter a new resource group name. - **Region**: Select an Azure location such as **Central US**.

notes.front: How many resource groups can one subscription hold?
notes.explanation: By contrast, the number of subscriptions associated with a Microsoft Entra tenant is unlimited.
notes.source: Microsoft, “Azure subscription and service limits, quotas, and constraints”, “Azure subscription limits” (MicrosoftDocs/azure-docs on GitHub)
notes.evidence: Azure subscriptions associated with a Microsoft Entra tenant | Unlimited | | Coadministrators per subscription | Unlimited | | Resource groups per subscription | 980

notes.front: How do you delete a resource group in the portal?
notes.back: Open the resource group and select Delete resource group.
notes.explanation: You open the group first, then choose the delete option on its page.
notes.source: Microsoft, “Use the Azure portal and Azure Resource Manager to manage resource groups”, “Delete resource groups” (MicrosoftDocs/azure-docs on GitHub)
notes.evidence: Open the resource group you want to delete. See Open resource groups. 1. Select **Delete resource group**.

notes.front: Can you move a resource group itself to a different subscription?
notes.back: No. You can move all its resources to a resource group in the other subscription instead.
notes.explanation: Tags, role assignments and policies on the original group don’t transfer automatically.
notes.source: Microsoft, “Move Azure resources to a new resource group or subscription”, “Can I move a resource group to a different subscription?” (MicrosoftDocs/azure-docs on GitHub)
notes.evidence: No, you can't move a resource group to a new subscription. But, you can move all resources in a resource group to a resource group in another subscription. Settings such as tags, role assignments, and policies don't transfer automatically from the original resource group to the destination resource group.

notes.front: When moving resources to a different subscription, what must the source and destination subscriptions share?
notes.back: The same Microsoft Entra tenant.
notes.explanation: You can check with Azure CLI or PowerShell that both subscriptions show the same tenant.
notes.source: Microsoft, “Move Azure resources to a new resource group or subscription”, “Checklist before moving resources” (MicrosoftDocs/azure-docs on GitHub)
notes.evidence: The source and destination subscriptions must exist within the same Microsoft Entra tenant. Use the Azure CLI or PowerShell to check that both subscriptions have the same tenant ID.

notes.front: A move between two subscriptions fails because they belong to different Microsoft Entra tenants. What are the two ways the documentation gives to reconcile them?
notes.back: Transfer billing ownership of the subscription, or associate the subscription with your Microsoft Entra tenant.
notes.explanation: Either route brings both subscriptions into one tenant, which a cross-subscription move requires.
notes.source: Microsoft, “Move Azure resources to a new resource group or subscription”, “Checklist before moving resources” (MicrosoftDocs/azure-docs on GitHub)
notes.evidence: If the tenant IDs for the source and destination subscriptions don't match, use the following methods to reconcile them: - Transfer billing ownership of an Azure subscription. - Associate or add an Azure subscription to your Microsoft Entra tenant.

notes.front: During a move from one resource group to another, a colleague tries to create a new resource in the source group. What happens, and what about the resources already there?
notes.back: The create fails, because both groups are locked; existing resources stay fully operational.
notes.explanation: While the move runs you can’t create, delete or update resources in either resource group.
notes.source: Microsoft, “Move Azure resources to a new resource group or subscription” (MicrosoftDocs/azure-docs on GitHub)
notes.evidence: During the move operation, both the source and target resource groups are locked. You can't create, delete, or update resources within these resource groups while the move is in progress. However, existing resources remain fully operational.

notes.front: How long can the resource group lock during a move last?
notes.back: Up to four hours, though most moves finish faster.
notes.explanation: The lock is removed as soon as the move completes.
notes.source: Microsoft, “Move Azure resources to a new resource group or subscription” (MicrosoftDocs/azure-docs on GitHub)
notes.evidence: The lock can last up to four hours. Most moves are completed faster, and the lock is removed accordingly.

notes.front: What happens to a resource’s identifier when you move it to another resource group or subscription?
notes.back: It changes.
notes.explanation: The subscription and resource group are part of the identifier’s path, so moving changes one or more of its values.
notes.source: Microsoft, “Move Azure resources to a new resource group or subscription”, “Changed resource ID” (MicrosoftDocs/azure-docs on GitHub)
notes.evidence: When you move a resource, you change its resource ID. The standard format for a resource ID is `/subscriptions/{subscriptionId}/resourceGroups/{resourceGroupName}/providers/{resourceProviderNamespace}/{resourceType}/{resourceName}`. When you move a resource to a new resource group or subscription, you change one or more values in that path.

notes.front: After you move a web app to a new resource group, an automation script that manages it starts failing. What should you check?
notes.back: Whether the script still uses the old resource identifier, which changed with the move.
notes.explanation: Any script or template that uses the resource’s identifier needs updating.
notes.source: Microsoft, “Move Azure resources to a new resource group or subscription”, “Changed resource ID” (MicrosoftDocs/azure-docs on GitHub)
notes.evidence: If you use the resource ID anywhere, change that value. For example, if you have a custom dashboard in the portal that references a resource ID, update that value. Look for any scripts or templates that need to be updated for the new resource ID.

notes.front: Does moving a resource to another resource group change its Azure region?
notes.back: No. It only changes the associated resource group, not the physical region.
notes.explanation: Dependencies with other resources can break, however, and might need to be configured again.
notes.source: Microsoft, “Move Azure resources to a new resource group or subscription” (MicrosoftDocs/azure-docs on GitHub)
notes.evidence: While moving a resource preserves its dependencies with child resources, dependencies with other resources can break and might need to be configured again. Moving a resource only changes its associated resource group and doesn't alter the physical region of the resource.

notes.front: Can resources be moved if a read-only lock exists on the source resource group, the destination resource group or the subscription?
notes.back: No. A read-only lock on any of them stops the move.
notes.explanation: Checking for such locks belongs among the steps before a move.
notes.source: Microsoft, “Move Azure resources to a new resource group or subscription” (MicrosoftDocs/azure-docs on GitHub)
notes.evidence: Azure resources can't be moved if a read-only lock exists on the source, destination resource group, or subscription.

notes.front: You move a resource that has an active Azure role assignment. What happens to the assignment?
notes.back: It doesn’t move and becomes orphaned; you must create it again after the move.
notes.explanation: Microsoft recommends removing it before the move, although the system removes orphaned assignments automatically.
notes.source: Microsoft, “Move Azure resources to a new resource group or subscription”, “Checklist before moving resources” (MicrosoftDocs/azure-docs on GitHub)
notes.evidence: If you move a resource with an active Azure role assignment (or its child resource with this same assignment), the role assignment doesn't move and becomes orphaned. You must create the role assignment again after the move. Although the system automatically removes the orphaned role assignment, we recommend that you remove it before the move.

notes.front: A resource and a resource it depends on sit in different resource groups, and both must go to another subscription. What must you do first?
notes.back: Bring them into the same resource group, then move them together.
notes.explanation: For a move across subscriptions, the resource and its dependent resources must be in one resource group and move together.
notes.source: Microsoft, “Move Azure resources to a new resource group or subscription”, “Checklist before moving resources” (MicrosoftDocs/azure-docs on GitHub)
notes.evidence: For a move across subscriptions, the resource and its dependent resources must be located in the same resource group and they must be moved together.

notes.front: How many resources in a single move operation make Resource Manager return an error immediately?
notes.back: More than 800; smaller moves can still fail by timing out.
notes.explanation: Microsoft advises splitting large moves into separate operations where possible.
notes.source: Microsoft, “Move Azure resources to a new resource group or subscription”, “How many resources can I move in one operation?” (MicrosoftDocs/azure-docs on GitHub)
notes.evidence: Separate large moves into different move operations when possible. Resource Manager immediately returns an error when there are more than 800 resources in a single operation. However, moving fewer than 800 resources can also fail by timing out.

notes.front: How can you test a move with the Azure CLI without actually moving anything?
notes.back: Use the `az resource invoke-action` command to validate the move.
notes.explanation: You need the identifiers of the source group, the target group and each resource you are moving.
notes.source: Microsoft, “Move Azure resources to a new resource group or subscription”, “Validate” (MicrosoftDocs/azure-docs on GitHub)
notes.evidence: To test your move scenario without actually moving resources in real time, use the az resource invoke-action command. Use this command only when you need to model the results without following through. To run this operation, you need the resource ID of the source resource group, target resource group, and each resource that you're moving.

notes.front: A subscription Owner who is not the account administrator wants to transfer billing ownership of a pay-as-you-go subscription. Can they?
notes.back: No. Only the account administrator of an account can transfer ownership of a subscription.
notes.explanation: In an Enterprise Agreement, the enterprise administrator transfers billing ownership between accounts instead.
notes.source: Microsoft, “Transfer billing ownership of an MOSP Azure subscription to another account” (MicrosoftDocs/azure-docs on GitHub)
notes.evidence: If you're an Enterprise Agreement (EA) customer, your enterprise administrator can transfer billing ownership of your subscriptions between accounts. Only the account administrator of an account can transfer ownership of a subscription.

notes.front: On a subscription’s page, which option starts a billing transfer, and whose email address do you enter?
notes.back: Transfer billing ownership; the email address of a billing administrator of the account that will own the subscription.
notes.explanation: The receiving account’s billing administrator is the person who reviews the request.
notes.source: Microsoft, “Transfer billing ownership of an MOSP Azure subscription to another account”, “Transfer billing ownership of an Azure subscription” (MicrosoftDocs/azure-docs on GitHub)
notes.evidence: On the Transfer billing ownership page, enter the email address of a user that is a billing administrator of the account that becomes the new owner for the subscription.

notes.front: How long is a subscription transfer request valid, and how many can be active at once?
notes.back: 15 days; only one request is active at a time.
notes.explanation: After the 15 days, the request expires.
notes.source: Microsoft, “Transfer billing ownership of an MOSP Azure subscription to another account”, “Cancel a transfer request” (MicrosoftDocs/azure-docs on GitHub)
notes.evidence: Only one transfer request is active at a time. A transfer request is valid for 15 days. After the 15 days, the transfer request expires.

notes.front: You transfer billing ownership and select Move subscription tenant. What happens to the existing Azure role assignments?
notes.back: They are all permanently removed.
notes.explanation: Only the user in the new account who accepts the transfer can then manage the subscription’s resources.
notes.source: Microsoft, “Transfer billing ownership of an MOSP Azure subscription to another account”, “Transfer billing ownership of an Azure subscription” (MicrosoftDocs/azure-docs on GitHub)
notes.evidence: If you choose to move the subscription to the new account's Microsoft Entra tenant, all Azure role assignments to access resources in the subscription are permanently removed. Only the user in the new account who accepts your transfer request will have access to manage resources in the subscription.

notes.front: Another company will pay for a subscription, but your team’s existing role assignments must keep working. What do you do with the Move subscription tenant option?
notes.back: Clear it, so billing ownership transfers without moving the subscription to the new account’s tenant.
notes.explanation: When the subscription stays in its tenant, existing Azure role assignments are maintained.
notes.source: Microsoft, “Transfer billing ownership of an MOSP Azure subscription to another account”, “Transfer billing ownership of an Azure subscription” (MicrosoftDocs/azure-docs on GitHub)
notes.evidence: Alternatively, you can clear the **Move subscription tenant** option to transfer billing ownership without moving the subscription to the new account's tenant. If you do so, existing Azure role assignments to access Azure resources will be maintained.

notes.front: When spending exceeds a budget threshold, what happens to the resources in scope?
notes.back: Nothing: resources aren’t affected and consumption isn’t stopped. Notifications are triggered.
notes.explanation: Budgets are for comparing and tracking spending as you analyse costs.
notes.source: Microsoft, “Tutorial: Create and manage budgets” (MicrosoftDocs/azure-docs on GitHub)
notes.evidence: Notifications are triggered when the budget thresholds are exceeded. Resources aren't affected, and your consumption isn't stopped. You can use budgets to compare and track spending as you analyze costs.

notes.front: A team expects its test resources to stop by themselves once a monthly budget is exceeded. Will the budget alone do that?
notes.back: No. A budget triggers notifications; resources aren’t affected and consumption isn’t stopped.
notes.explanation: The budget’s role is to notify people as spending crosses its thresholds.
notes.source: Microsoft, “Tutorial: Create and manage budgets” (MicrosoftDocs/azure-docs on GitHub)
notes.evidence: Notifications are triggered when the budget thresholds are exceeded. Resources aren't affected, and your consumption isn't stopped.

notes.front: How often are budgets evaluated against cost and usage data?
notes.back: Every 24 hours; cost and usage data is typically available within 8 to 24 hours.
notes.explanation: When a threshold is met, email notifications are normally sent within an hour of the evaluation.
notes.source: Microsoft, “Tutorial: Create and manage budgets” (MicrosoftDocs/azure-docs on GitHub)
notes.evidence: Cost and usage data is typically available within 8-24 hours and budgets are evaluated against these costs every 24 hours. Be sure to get familiar with Cost and usage data updates specifics. When a budget threshold is met, email notifications are normally sent within an hour of the evaluation.

notes.front: At the end of its period, what happens to a budget whose expiration date is still in the future?
notes.back: It resets automatically for the same budget amount.
notes.explanation: Because the amount stays the same, future periods that need different amounts need separate budgets.
notes.source: Microsoft, “Tutorial: Create and manage budgets” (MicrosoftDocs/azure-docs on GitHub)
notes.evidence: Budgets reset automatically at the end of a period (monthly, quarterly, or annually) for the same budget amount when you select an expiration date in the future. Because they reset with the same budget amount, you need to create separate budgets when budgeted currency amounts differ for future periods.

notes.front: How many cost thresholds and email addresses can one budget have?
notes.back: At least one threshold with an email address, and up to five thresholds and five email addresses.
notes.explanation: Each threshold is a percentage of the budget.
notes.source: Microsoft, “Tutorial: Create and manage budgets”, “Configure actual costs budget alerts” (MicrosoftDocs/azure-docs on GitHub)
notes.evidence: Budgets require at least one cost threshold (% of budget) and a corresponding email address. You can optionally include up to five thresholds and five email addresses in a single budget.

notes.front: Where do you create a budget for a subscription in the Azure portal?
notes.back: Open the subscription and select Budgets in its menu.
notes.explanation: The Scope pill lets you switch to a different scope, such as a management group.
notes.source: Microsoft, “Tutorial: Create and manage budgets”, “Create a budget in the Azure portal” (MicrosoftDocs/azure-docs on GitHub)
notes.evidence: To create or view a budget, open a scope in the Azure portal and select **Budgets** in the menu. For example, navigate to **Subscriptions**, select a subscription from the list, and then select **Budgets** in the menu. Use the **Scope** pill to switch to a different scope, like a management group, in Budgets.

notes.front: You want one budget in a subscription that tracks only the costs of a single service. How do you set it up?
notes.back: Add a filter for that service in the Create budget window.
notes.explanation: Filters let you create budgets on specific costs, such as a service or resource groups in a subscription.
notes.source: Microsoft, “Tutorial: Create and manage budgets”, “Create a budget in the Azure portal” (MicrosoftDocs/azure-docs on GitHub)
notes.evidence: Choose any filters that you want to add. Filters allow you to create budgets on specific costs, such as resource groups in a subscription or a service like virtual machines.

notes.front: Actual cost versus forecasted budget alerts: when is each generated?
notes.back: Actual: for cost already accrued against the thresholds. Forecasted: when the forecast cost projection exceeds the threshold.
notes.explanation: Forecasted alerts give advance notice that spending trends are likely to exceed the budget.
notes.source: Microsoft, “Tutorial: Create and manage budgets”, “Configure forecasted budget alerts” (MicrosoftDocs/azure-docs on GitHub)
notes.evidence: Actual costs budget alerts are generated for the actual cost accrued in relation to the budget thresholds configured. ## Configure forecasted budget alerts Forecasted alerts provide advanced notification that your spending trends are likely to exceed your budget. The alerts use forecasted cost predictions. Alerts are generated when the forecasted cost projection exceeds the set threshold.

notes.front: A manager wants a warning in mid-month if spending is on course to overrun, before the money is spent. Which budget alert fits?
notes.back: A forecasted budget alert.
notes.explanation: It uses forecast cost predictions rather than cost already accrued.
notes.source: Microsoft, “Tutorial: Create and manage budgets”, “Configure forecasted budget alerts” (MicrosoftDocs/azure-docs on GitHub)
notes.evidence: Forecasted alerts provide advanced notification that your spending trends are likely to exceed your budget. The alerts use forecasted cost predictions.

notes.front: For which scopes can a budget currently call an action group?
notes.back: Only subscription and resource group scopes.
notes.explanation: Through the action group you can also receive mobile push notifications when a threshold is met.
notes.source: Microsoft, “Tutorial: Create and manage budgets”, “Trigger an action group” (MicrosoftDocs/azure-docs on GitHub)
notes.evidence: You can receive mobile push notifications when your budget threshold is met by enabling Azure app push notifications while configuring the action group. Action groups are currently only supported for subscription and resource group scopes.

notes.front: When a subscription’s budget reaches 90%, several automated actions should run. What do you configure on the budget?
notes.back: An action group, which the budget calls when the threshold is met.
notes.explanation: The action group, not the budget, performs the actions.
notes.source: Microsoft, “Tutorial: Create and manage budgets”, “Trigger an action group” (MicrosoftDocs/azure-docs on GitHub)
notes.evidence: When you create or edit a budget for a subscription or resource group scope, you can configure it to call an action group. The action group can perform various actions when your budget threshold is met.

notes.front: Which type of Cost Management alert tells you that spending has reached or exceeded the amount in a budget’s alert condition?
notes.back: A budget alert.
notes.explanation: The spending can be measured on usage or on cost.
notes.source: Microsoft, “Use cost alerts to monitor usage and spending”, “Budget alerts” (MicrosoftDocs/azure-docs on GitHub)
notes.evidence: Budget alerts notify you when spending, based on usage or cost, reaches or exceeds the amount defined in the alert condition of the budget.

notes.front: Which Cost Management alert tracks the consumption of Azure Prepayment, and at what points is it generated?
notes.back: A credit alert, generated automatically at 90% and 100% of the Prepayment credit balance.
notes.explanation: Azure Prepayment is for organisations with Enterprise Agreements.
notes.source: Microsoft, “Use cost alerts to monitor usage and spending”, “Credit alerts” (MicrosoftDocs/azure-docs on GitHub)
notes.evidence: Credit alerts notify you when your Azure Prepayment (previously called monetary commitment) is consumed. Azure Prepayment is for organizations with Enterprise Agreements. Credit alerts are generated automatically at 90% and at 100% of your Azure Prepayment credit balance.

notes.front: Which Cost Management alert emails department owners when department spending reaches a fixed threshold of its quota?
notes.back: A department spending quota alert.
notes.explanation: The spending quotas themselves are configured in the Azure portal.
notes.source: Microsoft, “Use cost alerts to monitor usage and spending”, “Department spending quota alerts” (MicrosoftDocs/azure-docs on GitHub)
notes.evidence: Department spending quota alerts notify you when department spending reaches a fixed threshold of the quota. Spending quotas are configured in the Azure portal. Whenever a threshold is met it generates an email to department owners and is shown in cost alerts.

notes.front: Your organisation uses a pay-as-you-go (Web direct) offer. Which type of cost alert is available to it?
notes.back: Budget alerts only.
notes.choices:
A) Budget alerts only
B) Budget and credit alerts
C) Credit and department spending quota alerts
D) All three types
notes.choicesExplained: B and D include credit alerts, which pay-as-you-go offers don’t support. C names the two types that are for Enterprise Agreements only.
notes.explanation: Credit and department spending quota alerts are supported only for Enterprise Agreements.
notes.source: Microsoft, “Use cost alerts to monitor usage and spending”, “Supported alert features by offer categories” (MicrosoftDocs/azure-docs on GitHub)
notes.evidence: | Alert type | Enterprise Agreement | Microsoft Customer Agreement | Web direct/Pay-As-You-Go | |---|---|---|---| | Budget | ✔ | ✔ | ✔ | | Credit | ✔ |✘ | ✘ | | Department spending quota | ✔ | ✘ | ✘ |

notes.front: What does Azure Advisor analyse to produce its recommendations?
notes.back: Your resource configuration and usage telemetry.
notes.explanation: From that it recommends ways to improve cost effectiveness, performance, reliability and security.
notes.source: Microsoft, “Introduction to Azure Advisor”, “What is Advisor?” (MicrosoftDocs/azure-monitor-docs on GitHub)
notes.evidence: It analyzes your resource configuration and usage telemetry and then recommends solutions that can help you improve the cost effectiveness, performance, reliability, and security of your Azure resources.

notes.front: Which Advisor recommendation category aims to ensure and improve the continuity of business-critical applications?
notes.back: Reliability.
notes.explanation: It is one of the five categories on the Advisor dashboard.
notes.source: Microsoft, “Introduction to Azure Advisor”, “What is Advisor?” (MicrosoftDocs/azure-monitor-docs on GitHub)
notes.evidence: * **Reliability**: To ensure and improve the continuity of your business-critical applications.

notes.front: Which Advisor recommendation category detects threats and vulnerabilities that might lead to breaches?
notes.back: Security.
notes.explanation: Its recommendations target threats and vulnerabilities rather than spending or speed.
notes.source: Microsoft, “Introduction to Azure Advisor”, “What is Advisor?” (MicrosoftDocs/azure-monitor-docs on GitHub)
notes.evidence: * **Security**: To detect threats and vulnerabilities that might lead to security breaches.

notes.front: Which Advisor recommendation category aims to improve the speed of your applications?
notes.back: Performance.
notes.explanation: Its recommendations concern application speed.
notes.source: Microsoft, “Introduction to Azure Advisor”, “What is Advisor?” (MicrosoftDocs/azure-monitor-docs on GitHub)
notes.evidence: * **Performance**: To improve the speed of your applications.

notes.front: Your manager asks where Azure itself suggests ways to reduce overall spending across your subscriptions. Which Advisor category do you open?
notes.back: Cost.
notes.explanation: Cost recommendations aim to optimise and reduce overall Azure spending.
notes.source: Microsoft, “Introduction to Azure Advisor”, “What is Advisor?” (MicrosoftDocs/azure-monitor-docs on GitHub)
notes.evidence: * **Cost**: To optimize and reduce your overall Azure spending.

notes.front: Which Advisor recommendation category covers process and workflow efficiency, resource manageability and deployment best practices?
notes.back: Operational excellence.
notes.explanation: It is the category about how you run and deploy resources.
notes.source: Microsoft, “Introduction to Azure Advisor”, “What is Advisor?” (MicrosoftDocs/azure-monitor-docs on GitHub)
notes.evidence: * **Operational excellence**: To help you achieve process and workflow efficiency, resource manageability, and deployment best practices.

notes.front: After you implement an Advisor recommendation, how long can it take Advisor to recognise the action?
notes.back: Up to a day.
notes.explanation: Selecting the recommended action opens a simple interface for implementing it.
notes.source: Microsoft, “Introduction to Azure Advisor”, “What is Advisor?” (MicrosoftDocs/azure-monitor-docs on GitHub)
notes.evidence: Select the recommended action for a recommendation to implement the recommendation. A simple interface opens that enables you to implement the recommendation. It also might refer you to documentation that assists you with implementation. After you implement a recommendation, it can take up to a day for Advisor to recognize the action.

notes.front: How many levels deep can a management group tree go, and what does that limit leave out?
notes.back: Up to six levels, not counting the root level or the subscription level.
notes.explanation: The root and the subscriptions sit outside the six counted levels.
notes.source: Microsoft, “What are Azure management groups?”, “Important facts about management groups” (MicrosoftDocs/azure-docs on GitHub)
notes.evidence: A management group tree can support up to six levels of depth. This limit doesn't include the root level or the subscription level.

notes.front: A design has the root, then seven nested layers of management groups, then subscriptions. Is it allowed?
notes.back: No. Only six levels of management groups are allowed below the root.
notes.explanation: The root and subscription levels don’t count towards the six.
notes.source: Microsoft, “What are Azure management groups?”, “Important facts about management groups” (MicrosoftDocs/azure-docs on GitHub)
notes.evidence: A management group tree can support up to six levels of depth. This limit doesn't include the root level or the subscription level.

notes.front: How many management groups can a single directory support?
notes.explanation: However many there are, the tree holding them can be at most six levels deep.
notes.source: Microsoft, “What are Azure management groups?”, “Important facts about management groups” (MicrosoftDocs/azure-docs on GitHub)
notes.evidence: - A single directory can support 10,000 management groups. - A management group tree can support up to six levels of depth.

notes.front: Can a subscription sit under two management groups at once?
notes.back: No. A subscription can have only one parent management group.
notes.explanation: You can move subscriptions between management groups instead.
notes.source: Microsoft, “Manage your Azure subscriptions at scale with management groups”, “Move management groups and subscriptions” (MicrosoftDocs/azure-docs on GitHub)
notes.evidence: You can move subscriptions between management groups. A subscription can have only one parent management group.

notes.front: A subscription moves under a new management group. What does it inherit?
notes.back: All user access and policies from the parent management group.
notes.explanation: Only management groups and subscriptions can become children of a management group.
notes.source: Microsoft, “Manage your Azure subscriptions at scale with management groups”, “Move management groups and subscriptions” (MicrosoftDocs/azure-docs on GitHub)
notes.evidence: Only management groups and subscriptions can become children of another management group. A subscription that moves to a management group inherits all user access and policies from the parent management group.

notes.front: When you move a subscription to or from the root management group, do you need management group permissions on the root?
notes.back: No. The permission requirements don’t apply when the target or existing parent is the root.
notes.explanation: The root is the default landing spot for all new management groups and subscriptions.
notes.source: Microsoft, “What are Azure management groups?”, “Moving management groups and subscriptions” (MicrosoftDocs/azure-docs on GitHub)
notes.evidence: There's an exception: if the target or the existing parent management group is the root management group, the permission requirements don't apply. Because the root management group is the default landing spot for all new management groups and subscriptions, you don't need permissions on it to move an item.

notes.front: Your Owner role on a subscription is inherited from its current management group. Can you move the subscription to a management group where you are only a Contributor?
notes.back: No. You would lose ownership of the subscription; you can move it only to a management group where you are Owner.
notes.explanation: An inherited Owner role limits your move targets.
